prompt.value: A match predictor claims that he can predict the result of a match correctly x% of the time. It is agreed that his claim will be accepted if he correctly predicts the results of at least m of n matches. What is the probability that his claim gets rejected?

explanation.value: P(Correct match prediction)= p = x100Let, X be a random variable representing the number of correct match predictions. Hence, X∼Binomial(n,p ) The probability that his claim gets rejected is given by: P (X <m) = m−1∑ i=0 P (X =i) = m−1∑ i=0 nC i pi(1−p)n−i Suppose we substitute the values of x, m and n as 75, 5 and 6 respectively, then P(Correct match prediction)= p = 0.75 Let, X be a random variable representing the number of correct match predictions. Hence, X∼Binomial(6, 0.75) The probability that his claim gets rejected is given by: P (X <5) = 5−1∑ i=0 P (X =i) = 4∑ i=0 6C i 0.75i(1− 0.75)6−i = 0.466 Therefore, the probability that his claim gets rejected is 0.47 1

prompt.value: If X∼ Binomial(n,p ), then which of the following statement/s is/are always true? (n> 0 and 0 <p< 1)

explanation.value: If X∼Binomial(n,p ), then E(X) =np and Var (X) =np(1−p) When, 0 <p< 1 and n> 0, np>np (1−p)(always) Thus, option(d) is always true. For example: n = 1 and p = 12 np = 1× 12 = 12 and np(1−p) = 1× 12× 12 = 14 Since, 12 > 14 , thus E(X)>Var (X) Option (e) and (f) are not always true. For example: n = 3 and p = 12 Var (X) =np(1−p) = 3× 12× 12 = 34 = 0.75 S.D(X) = √ Var (X) = √ 0.75 = 0.87, which is greater than variance in this particular example. But, for n = 16 and p = 12 Var (X) =np(1−p) = 16× 12× 12 = 164 = 4 S.D(X) = √ Var (X) = √ 4 = 2, which is less than variance in this particular example. Hence, we can say that option (e) and (f) are not always true.
